Guide: Extending mizer

Source: vignettes/guide-extend-mizer.qmd

This guide covers the mechanisms for customising mizer’s dynamics without editing the package source, from external encounter and mortality through to whole new ecosystem components, with worked examples of each. To package an extension up for others to use, see the guide to creating a mizer extension package.

This is for changing how mizer works without editing the package source. Pick the lightest mechanism that expresses your change, and reach for a heavier one only when the lighter one cannot do the job. All setters return a new MizerParams — reassign the result.

Goal Use
Add a fixed external food or mortality source (no new state variable) ext_encounter() / ext_mort()
Add an extra encounter or mortality that depends on the model state but has no state of its own other_encounter() / other_mort()
Change how one built-in rate is calculated setRateFunction()
Add a new dynamical pool (detritus, carrion, oxygen, second resource…) setComponent()
Store parameters for your custom code other_params() (model-wide) or component_params (one component)
Extend plots/summaries for a custom model type S3 methods on an S3 extension class
Replace arbitrary internal mizer code (last resort) customFunction()

If you only need to change one rate, prefer setRateFunction() over replacing mizerRates() or patching internal functions. If you only need to change a number the rates are computed from, you do not need this skill at all — see the guide to changing model parameters.

External encounter and mortality (lightest)

For a background process that affects fish but needs no state of its own. Both are species × size arrays: ext_encounter (mass/year, added to getEncounter()) and ext_mort (1/year, added to mortality).

ext_mort(params) <- my_mort_array        # e.g. outside predators
ext_encounter(params) <- my_food_array   # extra unmodelled food

Build the array from the model’s own grid rather than from literal dimensions, so its shape and dimnames come out right, and add to what is already there rather than overwriting it. An extra food source scaling allometrically with body size:

params_ext <- NS_params
extra_food <- outer(rep(0.1, nrow(species_params(params_ext))),
                    w(params_ext)^(3/4))
ext_encounter(params_ext) <- ext_encounter(params_ext) + extra_food

This is the right choice when the extra process is not itself depleted or replenished, and the fish do not feed back on it. If it needs to respond to the fish, you need a component instead.

One such process is a species that you take out of the model but whose effect on the others you want to keep. removeSpecies(params, species, compensate = TRUE) adds what the removed species contributed to the encounter rate and mortality of the remaining species to their ext_encounter and ext_mort (and likewise external diffusion). It checks the remaining species’ effective equation rates and balances supported built-in resource dynamics. Extensions supply their own compensation through removal hooks; the operation does not establish that every component is at steady state.

External encounter changes the realised encounter and feeding level, but it does not enter the power-law reference state used by get_gamma_default() and get_f0_default(). Those defaults likewise exclude functions registered with other_encounter(), including a component’s encounter_fun: they describe feeding on the reference resource alone, before extra food sources are added.

If instead of adding food you replace the resource — a package that installs a resource system of its own — then any gamma mizer auto-derived at construction time is calibrated against a resource that is no longer in the model, and it will not be re-derived on its own. Give your class a measure_avail_energy() method, which is the hook both defaults use to look at the prey in the model, and rebuild the species parameters after installing your resources; see the section “But they do go through your get_*_default() method” in Creating a mizer extension package.

Replacing a rate function

Use when the model still follows mizer’s standard flow but one step should be computed differently — a time-dependent encounter, an alternative growth or recruitment formulation, and so on. Mizer stores the function name, so the function must be findable by name in the global environment or an installed package; a function defined inside another function cannot be found.

params <- setRateFunction(params, "Mort", "myMort")
getRateFunction(params)      # list the current rate functions

Replaceable rates include Rates, Encounter, FeedingLevel, PredRate, PredMort, Mort, ResourceMort, EReproAndGrowth, ERepro, EGrowth, Diffusion, FMort, RDI (density-independent recruitment), and RDD (density-dependent recruitment). Resource dynamics is set separately via resource_dynamics().

Write your function by starting from the built-in (mizerMort(), mizerEncounter(), …): copy it, change what you need, and keep the same signature and return dimensions/dimnames. Custom rate functions receive params, the current state (n, n_pp, n_other), t, and previously computed rates via ... — accept ... and pull what you need from it.

# Add a size-independent extra mortality, its size stored in other_params
myMort <- function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, f_mort, pred_mort, ...) {
    base <- mizerMort(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, f_mort, pred_mort, ...)
    base + other_params(params)$extra_mort  # a scalar or species × size array
}
other_params(params)$extra_mort <- 0.1     # store the parameter
params <- setRateFunction(params, "Mort", "myMort")

Time-dependent rates are the key reason to reach for setRateFunction(). Species parameters and rate arrays are fixed for the whole simulation, but a rate function receives the current time t and can therefore change as the run proceeds — seasonal forcing, a warming trend, a management measure that switches on in a given year. Wrap the built-in and scale its result by t:

seasonalMort <- function(params, t, ...) {
    mizerMort(params, t = t, ...) * (1 + 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * t))   # t in years
}
params <- setRateFunction(params, "Mort", "seasonalMort")

Under the second-order time steppers your function is evaluated a second time within each step, at t + dt and on a predicted state, so write it as a function of the t it is given: one that assumes time advances once per call, or caches the last t it saw, gives a different trajectory under project(method = "second_order") than under the default.

Never let a rate jump as a function of abundance. Depending on t or w discontinuously is fine; depending on n, n_pp or n_other discontinuously is not. Mizer’s time steppers freeze the rates during each density update, so they cannot see a threshold being crossed within a step. A rule like if (biomass < threshold) effort <- 0 gives a trajectory that keeps changing as dt is refined, makes solver = "newton" stall, and makes getStability() return a confident but meaningless answer — with no warning from mizer. Choosing method = "tr_bdf2" does not help. Give the switch a finite width instead:

# Bad: jumps. Good: ramps linearly between two thresholds.
frac <- (biomass - b_lim) / (b_trigger - b_lim)
effort <- effort * min(1, max(0, frac))

max()/min() kinks are continuous and much less troublesome — they cost some accuracy, not correctness. See the Discontinuous rate functions article.

Signatures and return shapes

Each replaceable rate has its own signature and its own expected return shape. setRateFunction() calls your function with test inputs at registration and checks the dimensions, so a mistake here surfaces immediately rather than mid-projection.

Rate Signature Return value
Encounter function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
FeedingLevel function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, encounter, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
EReproAndGrowth function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, encounter, feeding_level, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
ERepro function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, e, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
EGrowth function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, e_repro, e, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
PredRate function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, feeding_level, ...) numeric matrix, species × full size grid
PredMort function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, pred_rate, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
FMort function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, effort, e_growth, pred_mort, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
Mort function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, f_mort, pred_mort, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
RDI function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, e_growth, mort, e_repro, diffusion, ...) numeric vector, one value per species
RDD function(rdi, species_params, params, t, ...) numeric vector, one value per species
ResourceMort function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, pred_rate, ...) numeric vector, one value per full size bin
Diffusion function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, feeding_level, ...) numeric matrix, species × size
Rates function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, effort, rates_fns, ...) named list with all standard rate components

Three rules that follow from the table:

  • Return plain numeric objects. Never return an ArraySpeciesBySize or ArrayTimeBySpecies from a function registered with setRateFunction(); the get…() wrappers add those classes afterwards where they belong.
  • Most size-resolved rates match initialN(params) in both dimensions and dimnames. The exceptions are PredRate, which is on the full prey grid (w_full), and ResourceMort, which is one value per w_full bin rather than one per species.
  • Build outputs from existing mizer arrays so dimensions and dimnames are inherited. Most bugs in extension code are the right numbers in the wrong shape.

Respecting the model’s quadrature scheme

A model may be on either of two quadrature schemes, selected by the bin_average entry of second_order_w() (see the guide to running a mizer simulation). A model of defaults edition 3 or later is on the second-order scheme unless its creator chose otherwise; a model of an earlier edition, which includes NS_params and every model built with the default edition, is on the first-order one. Code that ignores this looks correct and passes tests run on such a model — and is then silently wrong by around 10% for anyone whose model is on the second-order scheme. Four rules:

  • Build derived quantities from the rate functions, don’t re-derive them. getEncounter(), getFeedingLevel(), getPredRate(), getEGrowth() already carry the right quadrature for whichever scheme the model is on. Re-deriving a rate from the species parameters is how this goes wrong.
  • To evaluate the encounter of a prey density of your own, use convolve_pred_kernel(). It is the convolution mizerEncounter() itself uses, with the kernel of whichever scheme the model is on. In a model of defaults edition 3 or later it zero-pads the grid, so the part of a kernel that falls below min_w_pp does not wrap around to the largest prey; in a model of an earlier edition it reproduces the circular convolution that mizer itself uses there. Its "predation" and "diffusion" kernels do the same for the predation rate and the predation diffusion. Never multiply the ft_pred_kernel_* slots by Fourier transforms of your own: in a model of edition 3 their length is not the length of w_full.
  • To write the encounter convolution out in full, use encounter_kernel(), not pred_kernel(). pred_kernel() returns the kernel point-sampled on the grid — right for plotting, and the form in which you supply a custom kernel, but not the bin-integrated coefficients the convolution consumes. Pair encounter_kernel() with the plain point prey weight w_full(params) * dw_full(params), which is a normalisation the kernel is built to cancel, so it must not itself be bin-averaged.
  • If your setter precomputes an array from a size-dependent parameter, gate it on params@second_order_w[["bin_average"]] the way setExtMort() and setResource() do, and do the integral once at setup so projection cost is unchanged.

For a summary-style integral \(\int N_i(w) K_i(w) dw\), do not write the sum at all: sizeIntegral(params, weighting = K, min_w = ..., max_w = ...) does the integral under whichever scheme the model is on and wraps the result — see “Writing your own indicator” in the guide to analysing and plotting mizer results. If you need the gating on its own, for a weight you are not integrating, that is bin_average_weight(K, params). Test any new integral with the flag on as well as off; a test on the default path alone proves nothing.

Adding a component

Use setComponent() for a new dynamical quantity — any R object: a scalar, a vector on the size grid, or a list. A component may contribute in up to three ways:

  • dynamics_fun — integrates the component’s state over a step, or rate_fun — supplies its derivative for mizer to integrate,
  • encounter_fun — adds to getEncounter(),
  • mort_fun — adds to getMort().
params <- setComponent(
    params, "detritus",
    initial_value    = 1e5,
    dynamics_fun     = "detritus_dynamics",
    encounter_fun    = "detritus_encounter",  # optional
    component_params = list(rho = 0.1)
)

Access components with getComponent(), remove them with removeComponent(). Component state is available to all custom functions as n_other[["detritus"]], and its parameters via component_params.

Reusable component definitions

You can collect the callbacks and plotting styles in a plain named list and reuse it across models:

detritus_definition <- list(
    dynamics_fun = "detritusDynamics",
    encounter_fun = "detritusEncounter",
    colour = "orange"
)
params <- setComponent(params, "detritus", initial_value = 1e5,
                       definition = detritus_definition,
                       component_params = list(rate = 1, capacity = 1e6))
getComponent(params, "detritus")$definition

The supported definition fields are dynamics_fun, rate_fun, encounter_fun, mort_fun, colour, linetype, integration_order, convergence_fun, role, stationary, equation_rates_fun, tuning, transformations, biomass_fun, biomass_filters, prescribed_mask_fun and autonomous. Supply a step, an equation, or both; a supplied custom step takes precedence during projection. Callback identifiers may be ordinary function names or package::exported_name. Mizer resolves them when preparing an operation. Initial state and component parameters are supplied separately. Assessment and tuning support are described below; measurement hooks remain under development.

Explicit arguments override the definition. A supplied definition replaces the old one: omitted encounter/mortality callbacks are removed and omitted styles default to grey/solid. Without a definition, a call patches only the arguments supplied, retaining the rest. Explicit NULL removes an optional callback:

params <- setComponent(params, "detritus", mort_fun = NULL)
params <- setComponent(params, "detritus", colour = "blue")

For an existing component, omitted initial state and component parameters are retained even when replacing its definition. The model stores the assembled definition, so editing detritus_definition afterwards does not change it. Apply a new definition explicitly with setComponent(), or in an extension’s upgrade method when migrating a saved model. The snapshot stores function names, not function bodies; the installed implementation of those functions still matters. Use getComponent(params, "detritus")$definition to inspect the stored choices. Ordinary setColours() and setLinetypes() updates keep those choices in step with the plotting settings.

If there is nothing for dynamics_fun to update — a starvation or senescence mortality reads the state but keeps none of its own — do not invent a component for it. Register the function on its own instead:

other_mort(params)[["starvation"]] <- "starvMort"
other_encounter(params)[["scavenging"]] <- "scavengingEncounter"

getMort() and getEncounter() add the result of every function registered this way, exactly as they do for a component’s mort_fun and encounter_fun. The two registries do not overlap: an entry that belongs to a component is owned by setComponent(), reported by getComponent() and removed by removeComponent(), and other_mort() deliberately does not list it — the same split other_params() makes for component parameters. Assigning NULL removes a free-standing entry.

The functions named in that call take the component’s name as a component argument, so one implementation can serve several components, and reach their own state as n_other[[component]] and their own parameters as params@other_params[[component]]. A dynamics function additionally receives the current rates and the step length dt, and returns the component’s new state — not a rate of change, so integrate the step yourself. This pair makes a detritus pool that fish eat and that relaxes back towards a capacity:

detritusEncounter <- function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, component, ...) {
    # The detritus is eaten through the same kernel and with the same
    # interaction as the resource
    prey <- n_other[[component]] * params@w_full * params@dw_full
    params@species_params$interaction_resource * params@search_vol *
        convolve_pred_kernel(params, prey)
}

detritusDynamics <- function(params, n_other, rates, dt, component, ...) {
    detritus <- n_other[[component]]
    p <- params@other_params[[component]]
    interaction <- params@species_params$interaction_resource
    mort <- as.vector(interaction %*% rates$pred_rate)
    target <- p$rate * p$capacity / (p$rate + mort)
    # Exact over the step, so the result does not depend on dt
    target - (target - detritus) * exp(-(p$rate + mort) * dt)
}

Convolving the component’s own abundance with the predation kernel, as detritusEncounter() does, is how to make a component act as an extra prey spectrum: it is then eaten through the ordinary predation kernel, under whichever quadrature scheme the model is on, and shows up as a column of its own in getDiet() without further work. An encounter_fun returns only the component’s own contribution, which getEncounter() adds to the rest. So do not delegate to mizerEncounter() with the component’s abundance as n_pp: mizerEncounter() returns the whole encounter rate, and the component would count the encounter of the fish and ext_encounter() a second time. convolve_pred_kernel() refuses a model with a custom predation kernel; there, write the sum out in full with encounter_kernel(), as described above.

Components and the time stepper

A rate_fun supplies the derivative of a finite numeric component state. Its return value must have the same length, dimensions and names as that state:

poolRate <- function(params, n_other, component, ...) {
    -params@other_params[[component]]$decay * n_other[[component]]
}
params <- setComponent(params, "pool", initial_value = 1,
                       rate_fun = "poolRate",
                       component_params = list(decay = 2))

Mizer applies Euler under method = "euler" and Heun under the second-order methods ("second_order", "tr_bdf2" and "predictor_corrector"). Heun evaluates the derivative at the start and at the full predicted endpoint, including the predicted states of other components and the endpoint rates. This handles both the component’s dependence on itself and its coupling to the rest of the model.

Heun is explicit. Selecting TR-BDF2 for fish does not give components a stiff solver, and growth-Courant subcycling does not provide a universal component stability bound. Retain a custom dynamics_fun for stiff, exactly integrable or non-numeric states. Supplying both capabilities uses the custom step for projection and makes the derivative available to diagnostics; the author is responsible for their consistency.

For the linear decay above, an exact custom step also works for a decay rate that is too stiff for explicit integration:

poolStep <- function(params, n_other, component, dt, ...) {
    n_other[[component]] * exp(-params@other_params[[component]]$decay * dt)
}
params <- setComponent(params, "pool", rate_fun = "poolRate",
                       dynamics_fun = "poolStep", integration_order = 2,
                       component_params = list(decay = 1000))

This step is exact for that independent linear equation. A more general custom step needs its own accuracy checks, including any coupling to other states.

A custom dynamics_fun still receives the start state, start time t and step length dt and must return the updated state. Under a second-order method it is called twice, once for the predictor and once for the corrector. Only the corrector’s result survives. Both calls advance the same interval, so callbacks must not accumulate changes in external mutable storage or assume one call per step. Custom resource dynamics follow the same convention.

The predictor receives the complete start rates. The corrector receives a complete effective midpoint list for all standard numeric rates, including pred_rate and f_mort. The consumer stepper keeps its specialised internal rate representation. Arbitrary extra fields in an extension’s rate list are not automatically averaged. Dynamics and diagnostic callbacks receive complete standard rates; ordinary single-rate getters retain their selective evaluation.

Custom component and resource steps can optionally accept predicted_state and endpoint_rates. The former is a list containing n, n_pp, n_other and t at the predicted endpoint; the latter is the rates evaluated there. These are predictions, not the final corrected state. Both are NULL when no prediction is available, including Euler and predictor calls. Legacy callbacks without these arguments or ... continue to receive their original arguments.

Passing better rates does not integrate the component’s self-dependence. A custom step written as state + dt * f(state, rates) remains first order. Integrate that dependence yourself, for example analytically for a relaxation process, or use rate_fun. A custom step that recomputes quantities from state can use predicted_state and endpoint_rates to form a consistent corrector.

The simulation’s sim_params$component_integration records the method and order used for each component: Euler/Heun for equations, or custom with an author-declared integration_order (unknown when omitted). This records the custom author’s declaration, not a numerical proof or a whole-model accuracy guarantee. Mixed order is permitted. If you replace a custom step, declare its order again rather than inheriting the previous function’s claim.

Test new dynamics by refining dt against an analytical solution or a suitably fine reference, including a genuinely coupled example. A second-order error should shrink by about a factor of four when dt is halved. Check stiffness separately. With subcycling enabled, callbacks receive the actual internal substep size and are called for each substep.

Components and the steady state

Register a convergence_fun when a component can assess whether its state is stationary. Biomass and derivatives do not supply this capability implicitly: the extension knows the meaningful measures and their tolerances. The callback receives the current state, complete standard rates, t, dt, the component name and its derivative when an equation is available (NULL otherwise). It returns a data frame with measure, value, tolerance and units columns:

poolConvergence <- function(params, n_other, component, derivative, ...) {
    data.frame(measure = "pool_change", value = derivative,
               tolerance = 1e-6, units = "g/year")
}
params <- setComponent(params, "pool", convergence_fun = "poolConvergence")

This example assumes a scalar pool with a registered rate_fun. A step-only component can calculate its own measure using its declared equations or an appropriate step comparison. Give every measure a unique, non-empty name; values must be finite and may be signed, and tolerances must be finite and non-negative. Mizer compares abs(value) with its tolerance while retaining the signed value. Multiple measures can use different units. Return quantitative measures, not a pre-combined boolean. A malformed result or callback error stops the operation with context.

getSteadyAssessment(params) returns the measures and whole-model coverage. isSteady(params) is TRUE when all required measures pass, FALSE when any fails, and NA when no failure is established but support is missing. A missing component measure stays missing even if its state happens to be unchanged. getSteadyResidual() remains a separate per-size diagnostic.

For an explicitly conditional assessment, name the dynamic blocks held fixed:

getSteadyAssessment(params, scope = "conditional", fixed = "component:pool")

The canonical IDs are consumers, resource and component:<name>. Conditional scope does not exempt any other unsupported block. A component with role = "prescribed" is instead a declared input of the model; do not use this role merely to silence a missing-assessment report. A temporary frozen step during tuning never changes the structural role.

Built-in consumers and resource use the same assessment contract. A custom resource must explicitly register its assessment with setProcess(params, "resource", convergence_fun = "myResourceConvergence"). getProcess() shows the stored specification. Process callbacks receive process in place of component. Provider bindings keep a declaration from silently following an incompatible replacement; re-register support explicitly after changing the implementation. Built-in resource_constant declares a prescribed resource.

Settling requires coverage of the requested scope before solving. Projection can evolve components when they have stepping support, while the current Newton solver requires unsupported dynamic components to be held fixed through an explicit conditional request. Every returned convergence report retains its scope; tuning reassesses restored dynamics before claiming a fixed point. ### Declaring prescribed coordinates and time dependence

Use prescribed_mask_fun on a component or state-owning process to exclude only part of a numeric state from equilibrium and stability analysis. The callback receives params and optional owner, component or process identifiers; it returns a logical array or vector matching the state’s dimensions and names exactly, without NA. TRUE denotes a structural input. The mask describes the model, not the current size of its derivative. role = "prescribed" denotes a wholly prescribed block. A caller holding an otherwise dynamic block fixed for one calculation instead requests conditional scope.

Convergence callbacks receive prescribed_mask and dynamic_mask for their owner. Apply the dynamic mask before forming quantitative measures; mizer cannot remove excluded coordinates from an already aggregated custom measure. The built-in consumer and resource assessments do this before integration.

A non-biomass state needs no artificial biomass measurement. For example, temperature can be assessed in degrees per year:

temperatureRate <- function(params, n_other, component, ...) {
    settings <- params@other_params[[component]]
    (settings$target - n_other[[component]]) / settings$tau
}
temperatureConvergence <- function(params, n_other, component, ...) {
    data.frame(measure = "temperature_change",
               value = temperatureRate(params, n_other, component),
               tolerance = 0.01, units = "degrees/year")
}
params <- setComponent(params, "temperature", initial_value = 15,
    rate_fun = "temperatureRate", convergence_fun = "temperatureConvergence",
    autonomous = TRUE, component_params = list(target = 15, tau = 1))

That declaration supports projection and assessment. Tuning or transforming the component still requires the corresponding declarations.

The independent autonomous declaration states whether the effective providers have explicit time dependence. Use TRUE only for time-independent providers, FALSE for forcing, and NULL for unknown support. Reproduction has no state of its own: its temporal dependence belongs to the consumers’ declaration. For continuous resource analysis, setProcess(params, "resource", rate_fun = "myResourceEquation") supplies the derivative in the shape of the resource state, with the complete current rate context. This is independent of the resource’s custom projection step.

These declarations have separate stored provider bindings. Updating a convergence callback does not renew a stale mask, equation or temporal declaration. Explicitly adopt each family that still applies after changing a provider. Arbitrary dynamic component coordinates are not yet supported by the stability Jacobians, even when equations are registered; whole-model reports then remain incomplete unless the caller explicitly requests a conditional subsystem.

Declaring tuning strategies

Projection, convergence assessment and tuning are separate capabilities. To support stationary tuning, declare stationary = TRUE explicitly, provide an equation_rates_fun, and register named strategies. A prescribed state alone does not establish stationarity: its effects on other processes could still depend on time. Time-dependent processes must provide an appropriate stationary formulation; mizer does not infer one by probing a few times.

For example, a pool that should evolve during tuning and needs no parameter adjustment can declare:

poolEquationRates <- function(params, n_other, component, ...) {
    pool <- params@other_params[[component]]
    list(source = pool$source, loss = pool$loss * n_other[[component]])
}
params <- setComponent(params, "pool", stationary = TRUE,
    equation_rates_fun = "poolEquationRates",
    tuning = list(default = "evolve", strategies = list(
        evolve = list(action = "none", evolve = "component:pool"))))

The equation callback returns a named list of finite numeric effective rates or equation terms, retaining their dimensions and names. Report independently adjustable inputs separately: reporting only source - loss would hide changes that cancel. It receives the shared rates, state, time and effort context; component callbacks also receive component. Core growth, diffusion, total mortality and final recruitment always get independent checks.

Each local strategy owns its process. Its hold$states and evolve partition the owned state blocks. Reproduction owns a rate, not a fictitious state, and can hold hold$rates = "consumers/recruitment". A balancing strategy supplies action = "balance", a named balance_fun, and adjust entries describing parameter paths, bounds and whether they are species vectors. For example:

adjust = list(source = list(path = c("other_params", "pool", "source"),
                            lower = 0, upper = Inf, species = FALSE))

Optional preserve entries select parameter paths or named callbacks returning quantities to retain. target_fun derives released equation targets from the constrained state before balancing; it must describe the constraints, not report targets chosen by the balancer. solvers lists supported operations ("project", "newton", "balance"), and partial_species = FALSE rejects partial requests. settings holds serialisable callback settings.

The balancer returns a candidate model. Mizer independently checks the target state, declared parameter changes and bounds, preserved quantities and all effective equation rates. It refreshes affected dependencies and reassesses the released model. There is no numerical fallback, silent clamp or second search to repair a failed balance.

Use setProcess() for the same declarations on "consumers", "resource" or "reproduction". Reproduction can also provide level_fun for its own level definition; it has no state role or convergence callback. Shared parameters require one joint strategy, registered with setTuningStrategy() and its explicit owners. A joint equation callback returns a named list of rate lists, one per owner. A selected joint strategy suppresses those owners’ local defaults; overlapping responsibilities or adjustable paths are errors.

Users can select alternatives with tuneSteadyState(params, strategies = c("component:pool" = "evolve")) or joint = "coupled". Declarations are stored with the model and bound to their effective named/S3 providers. Changing a provider requires explicit adoption of the corresponding support, not merely leaving an old function name in the registry.

When an extension changes mortality or encounter while preserving a built-in reproduction law, mizerReproductionDefinition(params) supplies its reusable strategy and level definitions. Explicitly adopt this through setProcess() only after checking the effective RDI/RDD route and its proportional dependence on erepro. The helper does not register support, validate an unknown wrapper or supply transformation declarations. A custom reproduction law needs its own specification.

Measuring component biomass

A component’s biomass_fun measures its stocks without defining convergence or changing the model. It receives params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, component and filters. Accept ... for arguments the callback does not need. Return finite nonnegative biomass in grams as a named numeric vector, or a data frame with series and value columns. Name a single value too, for example c(biomass = value). The richer form can also provide label, colour, linetype, source, available and reason; unavailable values must be NA with a reason.

poolBiomass <- function(params, n_other, component, ...) {
    stocks <- n_other[[component]]
    c(detritus = stocks$detritus, microbes = stocks$microbes)
}
params <- setComponent(
    params, "pool",
    initial_value = list(detritus = 20, microbes = 3, temperature = 15),
    dynamics_fun = "constant_other", biomass_fun = "poolBiomass"
)
getBiomass(params, include = "component:pool")

The default biomass_filters = character() declares only full-stock measurement. List supported filter names explicitly from min_w, max_w, min_l, max_l and use_cutoff; the callback must honour them. Unsupported filters produce unavailable measurements rather than silently returning the unfiltered stock. Only requested filters appear in filters.

Keep series identifiers, labels, styles and physical-source identifiers stable across saved simulation times. Use an unavailable row when a measurement is missing at one time. Distinct series default to distinct physical sources; if your component measures the built-in resource, declare source = "resource" so selecting both representations cannot double count it. Components without a biomass callback remain explicitly unavailable when requested.

Declaring mortality breakdowns

Additive contributions registered through mort_fun or other_mort() are included automatically by getMortByCause() when the outer mortality assembler is built in. A custom Rates or Mort provider instead registers setProcess(params, "consumers", mortality_fun = "myBreakdown"). This diagnostic capability is bound independently of convergence, tuning and transformation support; registering one family does not re-adopt another after a provider change.

The callback receives the model, state, effort, time, complete rates, authoritative total and process = "consumers". Return list(causes = list(...), complete = TRUE) with each named cause a finite species-by-size matrix. Optional metadata supplies id, label, owner, colour and linetype; optional unavailable rows explain missing causes of an incomplete report. Mizer checks complete causes against the actual total, cell by cell and time by time. Do not manufacture an attribution for unexplained mortality or use proportional rescaling to force agreement.

If the extension retains mizer’s ordinary mortality terms, its callback can start with mizerMortalityBreakdown() using the supplied context, append its own causes and metadata, and return the complete specification. This helper does not evaluate the rates again or validate the final sum; getMortByCause() performs that check after the author’s callback returns.

predation_by_species = TRUE requests a refinement into predator species. Mizer uses it only when those terms sum to the effective predation mortality; otherwise predation remains aggregated. The built-in callback uses one consistent grouping across selected simulation times. An author callback using the helper is responsible for keeping its returned series stable too.

Transforming extension data with the model

Species, grid and scale operations need their own capability. A component that can project or tune does not automatically know how its data should transform. Register a transformations map on its definition, or on a built-in process with setProcess(). The operation names are add_species, remove_species, reorder_species, rename_species, size_grid, scale_abundance and scale_rates. Missing support stops the operation before changes. Use list(action = "none") explicitly for an operation requiring no action.

An updating declaration supplies action = "update" and a named transform_fun. The callback receives the candidate params, the original model as before, operation, details, ownership context and any stored settings. It returns the updated candidate. Component callbacks receive component, and process callbacks receive process.

For example, a pool can contain a stock alongside an intensive temperature and a text label. Scaling should multiply only the stock:

scalePool <- function(params, before, component, details, ...) {
    state <- before@initial_n_other[[component]]
    state$stock <- state$stock * details$factor
    params@initial_n_other[[component]] <- state
    params
}
params <- setComponent(params, "mixed_pool",
    initial_value = list(stock = 2, temperature = 15, label = "inshore"),
    definition = list(dynamics_fun = "constant_other", role = "prescribed",
        stationary = TRUE,
        transformations = list(
            scale_abundance = list(action = "update", transform_fun = "scalePool"),
            scale_rates = list(action = "none"))))

A component owns its own initial state and component-parameter subtree by default. Declare additional permitted paths explicitly, as a list of character vectors naming fields in the model, when the hook must update other data it owns. Process hooks likewise declare their permitted paths. Mizer checks that hooks respect their declarations; it does not guess which dimensions represent species, sizes or biomass. Shared data require one joint declaration through setTransformation(params, name, owners, operation, definition). A registered joint hook replaces local hooks for those owners and that operation. Overlapping owners or writable paths are errors.

Species-operation details include old_species, new_species, species_map (old to new indices) and new_to_old (new to old indices); missing entries are NA. Renaming also supplies rename, a named old-to-new label vector. Grid details include old_w, new_w, old_w_full, new_w_full and their overlap maps: w_map, new_w_to_old, w_full_map, new_w_full_to_old. Scaling supplies factor. Use these explicit mappings to transform a species-by-size array such as spatial overlap; decide explicitly how newly added entries are initialised.

Hooks run after core structural bookkeeping and before dependent rate setters, initialisation or steady-state calculations. At this point the candidate is deliberately incomplete: other owners’ hooks may still be pending. Update only your declared data, using before when original values are needed; defer whole-model validation and dependent rate calculations to mizer. Coupled owners that need a coordinated update should use a joint hook. Errors leave the input model unchanged. The completed transformation retains its defaults edition and stored capability declarations.

When a process hook deliberately supplies a core rate array, declare that path explicitly. Its authored values are retained through dependent construction, including initial-state calculations. Update an authoritative predation kernel or its parameters, rather than its derived FFT caches. A manually supplied dense kernel or fishing array retains its overlap and freeze status through a grid change; new cells are zero unless the hook fills them.

Worked example: external encounter and mortality

The extra_food built above adds straight to the total encounter rate:

enc_base <- getEncounter(NS_params)
enc_ext <- getEncounter(params_ext)
range(enc_ext - enc_base, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 5.623413e-04 2.820537e+02

External mortality works the same way — note the negative exponent, since mortality falls with size where the extra food rose with it:

params_mort <- NS_params
extra_mort <- outer(rep(0.05, nrow(species_params(params_mort))),
                    w(params_mort)^(-1/4))
ext_mort(params_mort) <- ext_mort(params_mort) + extra_mort

Worked example: a seasonal encounter rate

Wrapping a built-in rate, in full. This one takes the amplitude and period of a seasonal cycle from other_params():

params <- NS_params
other_params(params) <- list(season_amplitude = 0.2, season_period = 1)
seasonalEncounter <- function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, ...) {
    p <- other_params(params)
    multiplier <- 1 + p$season_amplitude * sin(2 * pi * t / p$season_period)
    multiplier * mizerEncounter(params, n = n, n_pp = n_pp, n_other = n_other,
                                t = t, ...)
}

Registered by name, the rate now moves with t:

params2 <- setRateFunction(params, "Encounter", "seasonalEncounter")
enc0 <- getEncounter(params2, t = 0)
enc_quarter <- getEncounter(params2, t = 0.25)
range(enc_quarter / enc0, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 1.2 1.2

At t = 0.25 the multiplier is at its maximum, 1 + season_amplitude, exactly as intended. The seasonality then carries through a projection:

sim <- project(params2, t_max = 2, t_save = 0.1)
plotBiomass(sim)

A good first test for such a function checks that at t = 0 it agrees with mizerEncounter(), that at t = 0.25 it is scaled by 1 + season_amplitude, and that its result has the same dimensions and dimnames as initialN(params).

Worked example: a detritus-like component

Putting detritusEncounter() and detritusDynamics() from above to work. The component is stored on the full resource size grid, and starts at half the capacity it relaxes towards:

detritus_params <- list(capacity = initialNResource(params),
                        rate = params@rr_pp)

params3 <- setComponent(
    params,
    component = "Detritus",
    initial_value = initialNResource(params) / 2,
    dynamics_fun = "detritusDynamics",
    encounter_fun = "detritusEncounter",
    component_params = detritus_params,
    colour = "orange"
)

Its initial state is now in initialNOther(params3)$Detritus and its settings in getComponent(params3, "Detritus"). Because it is eaten through the ordinary predation kernel, it appears in the diet with no further work:

plotDiet(params3, species = "Cod")

The pool holds half the resource’s abundance at every size and is eaten with the resource’s interaction, so at every predator size its share of the diet is exactly half the resource’s — a quick check that an encounter_fun returns the component’s own contribution and nothing more:

diet <- getDiet(params3, proportion = FALSE)
range(diet[, , "Detritus"] / diet[, , "Resource"], na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 0.5 0.5

To let the component kill fish as well as feed them, give setComponent() a mort_fun too.

Extending plots and summaries: S3 methods on an S3 extension class

This is the most flexible route that still works with mizer’s public generics. MizerParams and MizerSim are S3 classes, and an extension package defines S3 methods for its own extension class — getBiomass.MyMizerSim(), plotBiomass.MyMizerSim(), summary.MyMizerParams() — which is what makes a summary or plot account for components the extension added. Every such method must call NextMethod(), so that several extensions loaded at once compose instead of overwriting each other.

Writing that package — the extension class, recording with recordExtension() and the methods — is the subject of the guide to creating a mizer extension package, and the order the methods then run in is the subject of the guide to using mizer extension packages.

Storing parameters

  • other_params(params)$foo <- value — model-wide parameters your custom functions can read.
  • component_params (a setComponent() argument) — parameters scoped to one component.

Keeping the two separate is what keeps params@other_params readable when several custom functions are in play.

customFunction() (last resort)

customFunction() replaces an internal mizer function inside the package namespace. Reach for it only after confirming that setRateFunction(), setComponent(), resource_dynamics()<- and setReproduction() cannot express the change: a replacement that is not fully compatible breaks the package, and nothing checks that it is.

Testing and packaging

  • Test both halves: that setRateFunction() or setComponent() succeeds, and that the downstream function you actually care about — getEncounter(), getDiet(), project() — uses your extension as intended.
  • An encounter function registered with setRateFunction() reaches getDiet() and getTrophicLevel() only through its total: they cannot know how your change is shared between the food sources, so they scale all of them in proportion and say so. That is exact for a factor that multiplies the whole encounter rate, like seasonalEncounter() above. For extra food, use a component with an encounter_fun instead, which getDiet() shows as a food source of its own. An extension package can give the exact split for any change, with a getEncounterByPrey() method; see the guide to creating a mizer extension package.
  • After registering a custom rate, run project() on a short horizon and check the affected get…() output looks right; write a testthat test that compares against a hand-computed value on a small model.
  • If a custom rate depends on the abundances through a threshold, read Discontinuous rate functions before trusting any results.
  • Once an extension is useful in more than one project, or you want to give it to someone else, make it a package: a stable namespace mizer can resolve function names in, somewhere for tests and documentation to live, and a version that gets recorded in the model metadata. Everything that only matters once you share — S3 extension classes, recordExtension(), dispatch via NextMethod(), bundled data objects, reporting through info_level, and upgrading objects saved by an earlier version — is in the guide to creating a mizer extension package. For the other side of it, loading and saving a model that needs an extension package, see the guide to using mizer extension packages.
  • For a larger design, it is worth discussing the interface on the mizer issue tracker before committing to it.
